subsection: 7. Representation and the Chemistry in Practice Investigation

notes.b: Chemistry describes the same event in three different ways: what you can see, what the particles are doing, and how we write it down. Good answers link all three.
points: The macroscopic (observable) level is what we see, measure and handle, for example ice melting, a solution changing colour, or gas bubbles forming. You need no special equipment to notice these changes.

The sub-microscopic (particulate) level is made up of atoms, ions (charged atoms), molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and electrons, and how they move and rearrange. These particles cannot be seen with a light microscope, which is why the level is called sub-microscopic.
The sub-microscopic level explains the observations at the macroscopic level: what we see happens because of what the particles do.
The symbolic level uses formulae, equations, diagrams and graphs to represent the particles and the changes, so that a change can be written down in a short, exact form.
Chemists move between the three levels: an explanation links what is seen to what the particles do, and writes it symbolically.
notes.tip: Never call the sub-microscopic level "microscopic", because the particles cannot be seen with a light microscope.

notes.h: Relating observations to particles: ice melting and magnesium in acid
notes.b: Each example runs from the observation, to the particle explanation, to the symbolic equation. These two show the full three-level pattern.
points: Ice melting, observed: a solid becomes a liquid at 0 °C at standard pressure (the agreed reference pressure for quoting melting points).

Ice melting, particles: water molecules gain energy and partly overcome hydrogen bonds (attractions between neighbouring water molecules), so they move past one another and the solid becomes a liquid.
Ice melting, symbolic: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l).
Magnesium in hydrochloric acid, observed: the solution fizzes and the magnesium disappears.

Magnesium in hydrochloric acid, particles: magnesium atoms lose electrons to form Mg²⁺ ions, and hydrogen ions gain electrons to form H₂ molecules. The H₂ is the gas that causes the fizzing, and the Mg²⁺ ions dissolve, so the metal disappears.
Magnesium in hydrochloric acid, symbolic: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain an observation in terms of particles and then write the equation. Give the hydrogen bonding in the ice example as a one-line explanation only.

notes.h: Relating observations to particles: flame colour and dissolving a salt
notes.b: Two more examples show how a simple observation is explained by the behaviour of electrons or ions.
points: A sodium salt in a flame, observed: a yellow-orange colour.

A sodium salt in a flame, particles: electrons in sodium atoms are excited (raised) to higher energy levels, and emit light of a specific energy as they fall back. That specific energy is what gives the colour.
A salt dissolving in water, observed: the solid disappears.
A salt dissolving in water, particles: water molecules surround and separate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (the charged particles that make up sodium chloride), so the solid breaks up and seems to vanish.
A salt dissolving in water, symbolic: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
notes.tip: Give flame-test detail only as a one-line example here. The sodium flame has no symbolic equation, so link it to the observation and the particle explanation.

notes.b: Particles are far too small to see, so chemists depend on pictures and models to understand them. Visualisation is a key part of understanding core concepts.
points: Chemists visualise particles they cannot see using drawings, physical models, animations and computer simulations.
Generating a model has steps: 1. Propose a representation that fits the observations.
2. Use the model to make a prediction.
3. Test the prediction.
4. After testing, keep, modify or discard the model, depending on whether the test supports it.

notes.b: Models are simplified representations of complex systems or phenomena; the three properties below apply to every model.
points: Simplified, with underlying assumptions: the kinetic theory (the model of gases as moving particles) assumes that gas particles have negligible volume and no forces between them. Real gases are more complicated, but the assumptions keep the model usable.

Modified as more data become available: the Bohr model of electrons in fixed energy levels was modified to the orbital model when it could not account for the spectra (patterns of light emitted) of atoms with more than one electron.

Predictive: VSEPR theory (a model of how electron pairs arrange themselves around an atom) predicts the bond angle in a molecule before it is measured, and the ideal gas equation predicts the volume of a gas.
notes.tip: A question may ask you to explain a statement about models using one example. Use the kinetic theory for simplified and the Bohr model for modified.

notes.b: Leaving Certificate Chemistry is assessed in two parts, so the investigation counts for a large share of the final grade.
points: Leaving Certificate Chemistry has two assessment components, both set and marked by the State Examinations Commission (SEC).
The written examination is worth 60% and is taken at Higher or Ordinary level, so students choose the level that suits them.

The Chemistry in Practice Investigation is worth 40%, or 200 marks. One common brief (the same task) is set for Higher and Ordinary level, and the investigation is assessed at the level at which the written paper is taken.
Grades are H1 to H8 at Higher level and O1 to O8 at Ordinary level, in bands of 10% from 30% to 100%; below 30% is grade 8.

The written examination uses a range of question types and assesses all four contextual strands (the main areas of the course), the unifying strand, and the application of chemistry to the cross-cutting themes of sustainability, health and technology.
notes.tip: The investigation is at a common level, not Higher and Ordinary. Know the weighting of each component and the level at which each is taken.

notes.b: The investigation starts from a brief, a document that tells students what the task is and gives them a context to work in.
points: The SEC publishes an Investigation Brief each year in term two of Year 1 (fifth year); the brief for the 2027 examination was issued in January 2026.
The 2027 brief asks students to investigate how the rate of a chemical reaction (how fast it happens) can be controlled, investigating one or more aspects of that topic.
The brief sets out the requirements and includes stimulus material (supplied information) that sets a context.
The brief allows students to develop their own ideas related to that context, and helps teachers and students to plan, so everyone knows what is expected before the work starts.
Students keep an investigative log (a running record of their work) that they draw on to write the report.
notes.tip: Do not invent the topic of any other year's brief. Only the 2027 brief is given here.

notes.b: The work has two strands, research and experiment, which together build an evidence-based argument in a final report.
points: Scientific research: students gather, process and evaluate information from secondary sources (existing published material, not their own results) on an issue related to the brief; this may inform the experimental work, for example by suggesting a hypothesis to test.
Experiment: students generate a hypothesis (a testable prediction) for an issue related to the brief, then plan and design the experiment.
Experiment: students carry out laboratory work to gather primary data (their own measurements), then analyse the data and form conclusions.
Students develop an evidence-based argument in response to the brief and submit a report in Year 2 (sixth year), in a format prescribed by the SEC.
The specification envisages up to 20 hours of work; a separate document, “Guidelines to support the Chemistry in Practice Investigation”, covers organisation.

Students give an authentic account of how the work unfolded, discuss the outcomes and say how they might revise the process. Engaging with the process matters more than a perfect answer, so an honest account of what went wrong is worth giving.
Experimental design, safety and measurement are part of the work. There is more on this in “Designing and conducting investigations” and “Measurement and error”.
notes.tip: If asked to describe the two main parts of the work, give the scientific research from secondary sources and the experiment, with its hypothesis, primary data and conclusions.

notes.b: The SEC brief allocates the 200 marks in four blocks of 50, one for each criterion (a standard the report is judged against).
points: Criterion A, 50 marks: title and introduction, background research and references.
Criterion B, 50 marks: designing and planning, and conducting the experiment, including safety, fairness, accuracy and choice of equipment.
Criterion C, 50 marks: data and data analysis, and conclusions, because the conclusions must follow from the data.

Criterion D, 50 marks: scientific literacy (communication, coherence, relevance and a reflective approach), judged across the whole report rather than in one section, because these qualities run through every part of it.
notes.tip: Do not invent section marks beyond these four criteria.

notes.h: The 2027 report: headings, format and rules
notes.b: The SEC also fixes the headings, limits and layout of the report, so students need to follow the format exactly.
points: The report uses seven numbered headings, each on a new page, so every section is easy to find: Title and Introduction; Background Research; Designing and Planning; Conducting the Experiment; Data and Data Analysis; Conclusions; References.
The report body is no more than 1,500 words (references, data tables, formulae, equations and labels are not counted), with no more than 20 images and no video.
Text is Arial and black, with 14-point bold headings and 12-point body text at 1.5 line spacing, portrait pages, 20 mm margins with nothing in them, and page numbers at the bottom centre.

The experiment and primary data collection are carried out under the direct supervision of the chemistry teacher, and every source, including any use of AI, is referenced, so the report shows where each idea came from.

The completed SEC cover page goes first; the report is converted to PDF, printed and proof-read, then given to the teacher by Friday 23 April 2027 with Authentication Form P.2 signed by the student, teacher and principal.
notes.tip: Do not invent word counts or submission dates. Use only the 2027 figures given here.

notes.h: How the investigation is judged: knowledge and design
notes.b: The NCCA descriptors of quality describe high and lower achievement in four areas: knowledge and understanding; investigative skills in design and method; investigative skills in analysis and conclusions; and relation to the work of scientists in society.
points: High achievement in knowledge and understanding shows considerable understanding of the brief, a clearly described purpose, and relevant research that evaluates a wide range of appropriate sources.
High achievement in knowledge and understanding also shows thorough engagement with the chemical concepts, explaining the phenomena clearly and accurately.
High achievement in design and method has a probing research question and a testable hypothesis underpinned by chemical concepts, so the experiment can genuinely support or reject the hypothesis.
High achievement in design and method has a thorough investigative design, with appropriate methods collecting high-quality primary data.

notes.h: How the investigation is judged: analysis, society and lower achievement
notes.b: The remaining two areas are analysis and conclusions, and relation to the work of scientists in society. The block ends with what lower achievement looks like.
points: High achievement in analysis and conclusions has clear, appropriate data and analysis, and valid conclusions justified by the data, so each conclusion rests on evidence, and related to the hypotheses.

High achievement in analysis and conclusions has a thorough evaluation that acknowledges limitations in the research, design and data gathering, because naming weaknesses shows the student understands how reliable the results are.
High achievement in analysis and conclusions has a summary of key areas and a coherent, consistent report with supporting references and reflections.
High achievement in relation to the work of scientists in society has a considered reflection that locates the outcomes within broader societal and scientific issues relating to the brief.
Lower achievement shows limited understanding of the brief, an unclear purpose, little research and a simple design, which means the work does little to answer the brief.
Lower achievement shows conclusions not linked to the data, no limitations identified, and few references or reflections.
notes.tip: The investigation is not examined in the written paper as a topic, but you need to know what the component requires.

keyTerms.definition: The level of observable properties, which we see, measure and handle.
The level of atoms, ions, molecules and electrons, and how they move and rearrange to explain observations.
The level of formulae, equations, diagrams and graphs that represent particles and changes.
A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms gains or loses electrons.
Using drawings, physical models, animations or simulations to represent particles that cannot be seen.
A condition accepted as true when building a model, which simplifies it so that it can be used.
A model that allows a behaviour or value to be predicted before it is measured.
The assessment component, worth 40%, in which students research an issue and carry out an experiment related to a common brief.
The document published each year by the SEC that sets the requirements and context for the Chemistry in Practice Investigation.
Material included in the brief to set a context for the investigation.
A dated, ongoing record of all experimental and research work that students draw on to write their report.
A source of information, such as a published article or database, that contains data collected by someone else.
The NCCA statements of what high and lower achievement look like in each of the four areas judged.
One Investigation Brief set for both Higher and Ordinary level students; the work is assessed at the level at which the written paper is taken.

questions.prompt: When magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, bubbles form and the magnesium disappears. Describe this change at the macroscopic, sub-microscopic and symbolic levels.
questions.model: Macroscopic: bubbles form, the solution fizzes and the magnesium ribbon disappears. Sub-microscopic: magnesium atoms lose electrons to form Mg²⁺ ions, and hydrogen ions in the acid gain electrons to form hydrogen molecules, H₂, which are the gas seen as bubbles. Symbolic: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).

questions.prompt: Using one example, explain each of the following statements about models: (i) a model is a simplified representation; (ii) a model can be modified as more data becomes available.
questions.model: (i) The kinetic theory is a simplified representation of a gas: it assumes that gas particles have negligible volume and no forces between them, which makes the model easy to use although real particles do have volume. (ii) The Bohr model of electrons in fixed energy levels was modified to the orbital model when it could not account for the spectra of atoms with more than one electron.

questions.prompt: Describe the two main parts of the work a student carries out for the Chemistry in Practice Investigation.
questions.model: The first part is scientific research on an issue related to the brief: the student gathers, processes and evaluates information from secondary sources, which may inform the experimental work. The second part is an experiment related to an issue in the brief: the student generates a hypothesis, plans and designs the experiment, carries out laboratory work to gather primary data, and analyses the data to form conclusions.

questions.prompt: State the weighting of each assessment component in Leaving Certificate Chemistry and the level at which each is taken.
questions.model: The written examination is worth 60% and is taken at Higher or Ordinary level. The Chemistry in Practice Investigation is worth 40%; it is set as one common brief for both levels and is assessed at the level at which the written paper is taken.
